fixes.concern: Two qualifier shifts vs. the source. (1) The source says a natural potassium deficiency is "highly unlikely"; the claim drops the intensifier to just "unlikely" (softening, akin to dropping "severely"). (2) The verbatim hedges "a potassium deficiency CAN be common in those individuals taking diuretics"; the claim strengthens this to "it BECOMES common in people taking diuretics", turning a possibility into an assertion (the documented "can"->"often" pattern). Both shifts flatten Wallach's hedges in opposite directions. Meaning is otherwise preserved; a faithful rewrite restores the two qualifiers.
fixes.original_claim_text: Dietary potassium deficiency is unlikely (grains, fruits, and vegetables are rich in it), but it becomes common in people taking diuretics for high blood pressure or weight loss.
fixes.proposed_edit: A natural potassium deficiency is highly unlikely (grains, fruits, and vegetables are rich in it), but a deficiency can be common in people taking diuretics for high blood pressure or weight loss.
fixes.verify_why: The original claim_text genuinely misrepresents the source on the hedge, so this clears the "leave-as-is" default. Decisive issue: source and the claim's OWN verbatim field both say potassium deficiency "can be common" in diuretic users, but the summary strengthened it to "becomes common" — converting a modal possibility into a categorical causal assertion (the documented can->becomes strengthening pattern), and directly contradicting the verbatim it is supposed to gloss. Strengthening a hedge is the dangerous direction for a health claim. The secondary shift (source "highly unlikely" -> summary "unlikely") is a minor softening I would tolerate alone, but the proposed edit restores it at no cost. I verified the proposed rewrite ("A natural potassium deficiency is highly unlikely (grains, fruits, and vegetables are rich in it), but a deficiency can be common in people taking diuretics for high blood pressure or weight loss") against source_span_pm3500: every clause traces faithfully, it restores both qualifiers plus source's "natural," and introduces no new error. Faithful, meaning-preserving fidelity correction — not an over-eager rewrite.
